:::{#thm-schur-test}
#### Schur complement test

Let $\matr{X} = \begin{bmatrix} \matr{A} & \matr{B} \\ \tp{\matr{B}} & \matr{C} \end{bmatrix}$
be as in @thm-block-quadratic.
Then $\matr{X}$ is positive definite (@def-positive-definite)
exactly when $\matr{A}$ is positive definite
and its Schur complement $\matr{S}$ (@def-schur-complement) is positive definite.

:::

::: proof

**If.**
$\matr{A}$ is positive definite, so invertible (@thm-pd-inverse), and $\matr{S}$ is defined.
$\matr{X}$ is symmetric.
Let $\vx = (\vecf{u}, \vecf{w}) \ne \vzero$ and $\vecf{z} = \vecf{u} + \matr{A}^{-1} \matr{B} \vecf{w}$.
By @thm-block-quadratic, $\tp{\vx} \matr{X} \vx = \tp{\vecf{z}} \matr{A} \vecf{z} + \tp{\vecf{w}} \matr{S} \vecf{w}$,
and both terms are at least $0$.
If $\vecf{w} \ne \vzero$, the second term is positive.
If $\vecf{w} = \vzero$, then $\vecf{u} \ne \vzero$ and $\vecf{z} = \vecf{u}$, so the first term is positive.
Either way $\tp{\vx} \matr{X} \vx > 0$.

**Only if.**
$\matr{A}$ is the top-left $k \times k$ block of $\matr{X}$, so it is positive definite (@thm-pd-submatrix),
and invertible (@thm-pd-inverse).
$\matr{S}$ is symmetric:
$\tp{(\tp{\matr{B}} \matr{A}^{-1} \matr{B})} = \tp{\matr{B}}\,\tp{(\matr{A}^{-1})}\,\matr{B} = \tp{\matr{B}} \matr{A}^{-1} \matr{B}$
(@thm-transpose-product, @def-matrix-transpose for $\tp{(\tp{\matr{B}})} = \matr{B}$, @cor-inverse-symmetric),
and $\matr{C}$ is symmetric,
so $\matr{S} = \matr{C} - \tp{\matr{B}} \matr{A}^{-1} \matr{B}$ is symmetric
(the transpose of a difference is the difference of the transposes, entry by entry, @def-matrix-transpose).
For $\vecf{w} \ne \vzero$, take $\vecf{u} = -\matr{A}^{-1} \matr{B} \vecf{w}$, so $\vecf{z} = \vzero$
and $\vx = (\vecf{u}, \vecf{w}) \ne \vzero$; then
$\tp{\vecf{w}} \matr{S} \vecf{w} = \tp{\vx} \matr{X} \vx > 0$ (@thm-block-quadratic).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-schur-test}
#### Testing $2 \times 2$ matrices

A symmetric $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{bmatrix}$ is positive definite
exactly when $a > 0$ and $c - \tfrac{b^2}{a} > 0$, that is, $a > 0$ and $ac > b^2$
(a $1 \times 1$ matrix $[s]$ is positive definite exactly when $s > 0$, since $\tp{x} s x = s x^2$).

- $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$: $5 > 0$ and $\tfrac{9}{5} > 0$ (@exm-schur-complement),
  so it is positive definite.
- $\matr{D} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$: $1 > 0$ but $\matr{S} = -3$,
  so it is not, as @exm-positive-definite found directly.

:::
